newsitem.title: USA: Alaska board resigns from Yukon Quest race.
newsitem.headline: Alaska board resigns from Yukon Quest race.

text.p: The entire Alaska board of the Yukon Quest International resigned on Tuesday, citing a widening rift between their organization and the Canadian board that co-manages the 1,000-mile (1,609 km) sled dog race between Fairbanks, Alaska, and Whitehorse in the Yukon.

"The Yukon Quest Alaska Board has decided that turmoil and uncertainty is harmful to dog mushing," said a letter signed by all six Alaska board members and the race's Fairbanks-based executive director.
The resignations were announced four days after the Alaska board declared plans to cut Whitehorse out of the race route and the Yukon board out of the event's management.

But on Tuesday, Alaska executive director Phil Cole said an altered sled-dog race route -- a proposal that drew bitter opposition from mushers and Yukon Quest fans -- was never really a serious proposal.
Instead, it was a move "like dropping the bomb" that was intended to draw attention to a dispute over terms of a sponsorship contract negotiated by the Whitehorse-based Yukon board, Cole said.
The disputed contract is from Fulda, a German tire maker, he said.
"This contract was negotiated and then signed without any knowledge from the Alaska board, although the Alaska portion was obligated to the terms and conditions of that contract," he said.
Sixteen mushers are signed up to compete in the 1998 Yukon Quest, Cole said. If the race is held as planned, it will be the 15th running of the event.
"I would definitely hope that the race is on as planned," Cole said.
However, the Yukon Quest is $45,000 to $49,000 in debt, he said.
Confusion over the fate of the Yukon Quest -- an event often overshadowed by the more famous Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race -- appeared to be widespread Tuesday.
Members of the race's Yukon board were in Fairbanks holding public meetings on the race's future.
Telephone calls to the local daily newspaper, the Fairbanks Daily News-Miner, ran 6-1 against changing the race route, according to reports by the Alaska Public Radio Network.
